listenings.text: Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. Thank you again for the tour of the distribution center yesterday. My editor has already read the first draft, and she loved it. I have just two questions before I finish. I wrote that the vaccines are kept at two to eight degrees, but are they checked again before they are dispatched? And the shipment that was held up at the port on Tuesday, has it been cleared yet? One more thing. You told me that nothing is done by hand anymore. My readers will love that line, but I need to be sure it is true. I would like to send the piece to my editor on Friday, so call me when you can.

Welcome back to The Long Game. Today, a grammar point that every manager uses and almost nobody notices: the passive. Listen to two sentences. Our team dispatched the order at six. The order was dispatched at six. Same fact, different focus. In the first sentence, the hero is the team. In the second, the hero is the order. When you describe a process, the object is usually more important than the person, so the passive sounds natural. The boxes are scanned, the trucks are loaded, the batch has been released. But be careful, because the passive can also be used to hide. Mistakes were made. By whom? If you are the director and something went wrong, say who did it, especially if it was you. That is what people trust. So here is the rule for this week: use the passive for processes, and the active for responsibility.

extra_audio.text: First, the batch is received and every box is scanned. Then, it is stored in the cold room at two to eight degrees. Next, the temperature is recorded every five minutes. After that, the order is checked and loaded onto a truck. Finally, the batch is dispatched to the pharmacies.
